tasks.title: Build a deterministic, sanitized tenant database name
tasks.description: Write tenant_db_name(int $tenantId): string — returns a deterministic, database-name-safe name of the form 'tenant_<zero-padded-id>'. Example: tenant_db_name(7) returns 'tenant_000007'; tenant_db_name(12345) returns 'tenant_012345'.

tasks.title: filter_by_tenant leaks rows owned by other tenants
tasks.description: filter_by_tenant(array $rows, int $tenantId): array must return ONLY the rows whose tenant_id strictly equals $tenantId, preserving their original order. Hint: the current check scans every field of each row instead of just the tenant_id column, so a row whose id (or any other field) happens to equal the tenant id leaks into the result — a cross-tenant data leak.

tasks.title: Design a data-leak-proof multi-tenant Laravel SaaS
tasks.description: Design a multi-tenant Laravel SaaS. Choose an isolation model (shared database with tenant_id vs database-per-tenant vs schema-per-tenant), explain tenant resolution, how migrations behave under your model, how queues and cache stay tenant-aware, and how you prevent cross-tenant data leaks. Weigh trade-offs and defend your choice.
tasks.solution:
Default to a shared database with a tenant_id column for most B2B SaaS workloads; reserve database-per-tenant or schema-per-tenant for customers with hard isolation requirements (regulated data, per-tenant backup/retention SLAs) where the extra cost is justified. With a shared schema, add tenant_id to every tenant-owned table, include it in composite unique keys so a unique slug can repeat across tenants, and add it to foreign keys where the DB engine allows. Never rely on app code alone: install a Laravel global scope that injects where tenant_id = ? into every model query, so a forgotten ->where() or an eager-loaded relation cannot silently return another tenant's rows.

Resolve the tenant in middleware from the subdomain or the authenticated user, never from a client-controlled body parameter, and bind the resolved Tenant into the container (e.g. a TenantContext singleton) for the whole request. Queued jobs are a classic leak vector: serialize tenant_id onto the job payload and, in a queue middleware, re-resolve and rebind the tenant context before the job executes. Cache and session keys must be tenant-scoped as well — cache()->tags() or a tenant:{id}: key prefix — because a shared cache key is a cross-tenant leak of the same severity as a shared DB row.

Migrations depend on the model: a shared schema migrates once, centrally. Database- or schema-per-tenant requires per-tenant migration runners, per-tenant connection configuration, runtime connection swapping, and a strict first/last-tenant migration discipline — an operational tax usually not worth paying until isolation is an actual product requirement. Finally, prevent leaks with defense in depth: global scopes, a tenant-aware query layer, DB constraints that include tenant_id, and integration tests asserting Tenant A can never read Tenant B's rows, including soft-deleted records and eager-loaded relations.

criteria: Isolation-model choice is justified against the product's isolation, compliance, and scaling requirements — not picked by default.
Tenant resolution (subdomain/authenticated user, middleware, container-bound context) is described, including why client-controlled tenant ids are rejected.
Migrations strategy matches the chosen model: central single-schema migrations versus per-tenant migration runners and connection handling.
Tenant-awareness of queues (tenant_id on the job + rebinding middleware) and tenant-scoped cache/session keys are covered.
Data-leak prevention is defense-in-depth: global scopes, DB constraints including tenant_id, and cross-tenant integration tests.
key_points: Shared DB with tenant_id is the sensible default; db/schema-per-tenant only for genuine isolation or compliance requirements.
Tenant identity comes from request context (subdomain/auth), never from client input.
Global scopes make tenant filtering automatic so a missing ->where() cannot leak data.
Queues and cache are leak vectors too: bind tenant_id to jobs and prefix or partition cache keys.
Enforce tenant_id in unique/foreign-key constraints and prove isolation with cross-tenant tests.
